title: Intervals
summary: Sort by start or end, then merge, sweep, or pick with a greedy scan.

body:
Rule. Store each interval as a start and an end. Sort by start when merging overlaps; sort by end when selecting the maximum non-overlapping subset. A sweep processes start and end events in time order while tracking how many intervals are live. After the sort, one linear scan usually finishes the job. Name the sort key before writing the loop.

Why it matters. Calendar merges, room counts, and coverage problems look chaotic until ordered. Scanning unsorted pairs misses merges; the wrong sort key breaks the greedy proof. Interviewers listen for which endpoint you sort on before you write the loop, because that choice encodes the algorithm.

Worked example. Merge [1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18]. Sorted by start already. Seed current=[1,3]. Next [2,6] overlaps because 2 ≤ 3, so raise the current end to max(3,6)=6. Next [8,10] starts after 6: emit [1,6] and shift current to [8,10]. Next [15,18]: emit [8,10], shift to [15,18], then emit the last interval. Result is [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]. For meeting-room count on [0,30], [5,10], [15,20], turn starts and ends into events, sort them, and sweep while counting active meetings; the peak active value is 2 during the early overlap between [0,30] and [5,10].

[[diagram:overlap]]

When to use. Merge when you must simplify overlapping ranges. Use earliest-finish greedy for the largest non-overlapping subset. Use a sweep to find peak overlap or resource demand. Sort by start when a left-to-right merge scan is the plan.

When to refuse. Do not process intervals unsorted. Do not merge when the ask is maximum non-overlapping count (that wants finish-time greedy). Do not assume closed versus half-open endpoints without matching the problem. Do not fall back to pairwise quadratic checks when sort-plus-scan works.
